title: Zagreb Orders HVO Ceasefire With ARBiH
narrative: Tuđman accepts a US-brokered ceasefire arrangement and orders Boban to stand down HVO operations against ARBiH. Croatia's EU trajectory and the threat of US sanctions leave Zagreb no choice — the Washington Agreement framework serves Croatian interests better than continued war.
historical_source: Washington Agreement, 1 March 1994; ICTY Prlić et al. IT-04-74-T Trial Judgment (29 May 2013) Vol. 1 §§357-422 and §§556-590 (HZ HB Presidency-Zagreb axis directing the February 1994 ceasefire posture and the Washington Agreement framework preconditions); Vol. 2 §§600-680 (Tudjman-Boban coordination through the Granic-Silajdzic diplomatic channel preceding the 23 February 1994 ceasefire); Granić, Vanjski poslovi (2005) — Granić-Šilajdžić channel record; Tudjman Presidential Transcripts admitted at Prlić (February 1994 set); US State Department Christopher/Redman shuttle records, February 1994; Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II pp. 506-520.
source_note: The February 1994 Zagreb ceasefire order follows the Washington track: with Croatia's EU trajectory and credible US sanctions on the table, Tudjman directs Boban via the Granic-Silajdzic channel to stand down HVO operations against ARBiH (Prlic Vol. 1 §§357-422; Vol. 2 §§556-590, §§600-680; Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II pp. 506-520). Acknowledge-pressure is the documented historical posture — Boban accepted the directive, opening the Washington Agreement signature window (1 March 1994). Resist-patron is a structurally plausible counterfactual grounded in the analogous patron-resistance precedent at R6 (RS Assembly rejection of VOPP, 5-6 May 1993).

effect.text: Tuđman orders Boban to stand down HVO operations against ARBiH under the Washington Agreement framework.

title: First Markale Massacre
narrative: A mortar shell strikes the Markale marketplace in Sarajevo, killing 68 civilians and wounding over 140. The images of carnage broadcast worldwide provoke outrage and push NATO toward its first decisive action in the Bosnian war. The VRS denies responsibility, but the international community overwhelmingly attributes the attack to Serb forces.
source_note: Existing ICTY/UN and same-id essay sources ground the row's provenance and institutional context. This note adds no casualty figures, causal claims, prohibited player choices, or alternate-outcome prevention framing.

effects.text: The Markale massacre kills 68 civilians. The atrocity becomes the catalyst for NATO's ultimatum to the VRS.

title: NATO Issues Ultimatum on Sarajevo
narrative: In the aftermath of Markale, NATO issues an ultimatum demanding the withdrawal of all VRS heavy weapons from a 20-kilometer exclusion zone around Sarajevo within ten days, or face air strikes. The ultimatum marks NATO's first credible threat of force and fundamentally changes the calculation for the VRS around the capital. This is a pivotal moment — compliance eases international pressure, defiance risks becoming the first belligerent to face NATO bombing.

effects.text: NATO demands VRS withdrawal of heavy weapons from around Sarajevo. The threat of air strikes becomes credible for the first time.

response_options.label: Comply — withdraw heavy weapons from the exclusion zone
Defy — maintain all positions around Sarajevo

RBiH.headline: VRS accepts Sarajevo heavy-weapons ultimatum
RBiH.body: RS agrees to pull heavy weapons back from the Sarajevo exclusion zone or place them under UN control. Sarajevo sees immediate shelling pressure ease, while the siege itself remains unresolved.

HRHB.headline: VRS complies with NATO ultimatum
HRHB.body: RS accepts the heavy-weapons withdrawal demand around Sarajevo. Mostar sees NATO coercion work at the capital, with VRS military credibility taking a visible cost.

RBiH.headline: VRS defies Sarajevo ultimatum
RBiH.body: RS keeps heavy weapons around Sarajevo despite NATO's deadline. Sarajevo faces continued siege pressure, while the risk of air strikes and wider intervention rises.

HRHB.headline: VRS rejects NATO heavy-weapons demand
HRHB.body: RS refuses to withdraw heavy weapons from the Sarajevo exclusion zone. Mostar sees Pale preserve battlefield posture while accepting a sharper confrontation with NATO.

title: NATO Ultimatum — Sarajevo HWEZ Compliance
narrative: Following the North Atlantic Council decision of 9 February 1994, NATO demands the withdrawal of all heavy weapons from a 20-kilometer exclusion zone around Sarajevo by 0001Z on 21 February 1994 or face air strikes. The Heavy Weapons Exclusion Zone regime is symmetric: it applies to VRS positions and to any ARBiH heavy weapons inside the perimeter. The Sarajevo Presidency must record its posture toward the symmetric framing — cooperation with UNPROFOR collection-point inventories, or refusal of the moral-equivalence of withdrawal demands on the besieging army and the defenders.
historical_source: NATO North Atlantic Council decision of 9 February 1994 (Heavy Weapons Exclusion Zone ultimatum, NATO Final Communiqué; UN S/1994/154); UN Security Council Resolution 836 (4 June 1993) authorizing UNPROFOR use of force in support of safe areas; UN Security Council Resolution 824 (6 May 1993) declaring Sarajevo a safe area; UN Secretary-General report on the fall of Srebrenica A/54/549 (15 November 1999) §§ on the Sarajevo HWEZ regime; UN Secretary-General reports on UNPROFOR (S/1994/300 series) documenting HWEZ compliance and verification; ICTY Galić Trial Judgement IT-98-29-T (5 December 2003) and Appeal Judgement (30 November 2006) fixing Markale 5 February 1994 attribution to SRK/VRS positions; ICTY Mladić Trial Judgement IT-09-92-T (22 November 2017) on SRK siege as JCE instrument and NATO-enforcement context; ICTY Dragomir Milošević Trial Judgement IT-98-29/1 (12 December 2007); ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgement IT-95-5/18-T (24 March 2016) on Sarajevo siege at RS leadership level; Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II Sarajevo HWEZ chronology.
source_note: RBiH-side companion to existing nato_ultimatum_sarajevo_1994 (RS-facing, sensitive-gated). Per Phase A B9 worksheet (docs/40_reports/research/20260527_EVENT_FAMILY_B9.md) and Wave 1 B-B batch + Phase A vocabulary namespacing decision, this row is a separate RBiH-facing decision event with distinct option ids (rbih_comply_hwez_regime, rbih_defy_hwez_regime) to prevent collision with the RS-side comply_withdraw_hwez/defy_ultimatum_hwez option ids. Branch flags: event_flags.rbih_nato_response = 'comply'|'defy' are distinct from sarajevo_hwez_complied (RS-set). Historical Presidency posture (Izetbegović + Sarajevo Assembly): public framing of NATO action as overdue Western coercion + cooperation with UNPROFOR inspections + acceptance of symmetric application of HWEZ to ARBiH (relatively few heavy weapons inside the perimeter; asymmetric material cost). The counterfactual defy branch is defensible as a posture-of-protest counterfactual sourced in Assembly-debate currents at the time; it was not the documented action of the Presidency.
staff_assessment: Comply with the NATO ultimatum and accept the symmetric HWEZ application: cooperate with UNPROFOR collection-point inventories, withdraw any ARBiH heavy weapons inside the 20km perimeter, publicly support NATO enforcement against the VRS. This is the documented Sarajevo posture (Presidency cooperation with HWEZ regime; 12 February 1994 first-day-without-casualty since April 1992 publicly owned as vindication). Defying the ultimatum to protest the moral-equivalence framing would carry significant negotiating-leverage and international-standing costs while jeopardizing the federation and Washington track that arrives in March.
trigger_evidence: The Markale market shelling of 5 February 1994 has fixed Sarajevo as the casus belli for Western coercion against the VRS.
The North Atlantic Council ultimatum of 9 February 1994 applies symmetrically to ARBiH heavy weapons inside the 20km Sarajevo exclusion zone.
The Presidency must record its posture toward the symmetric framing before the 21 February 1994 deadline.

effect.text: The Sarajevo Presidency convenes to record its posture toward the NATO Heavy Weapons Exclusion Zone regime.

effects.text: Izetbegović, Silajdžić, and the Assembly inner circle weigh cooperation with UNPROFOR HWEZ inventories against the symmetric framing's moral-equivalence cost.

response_options.label: Withdraw ARBiH heavy weapons from the HWEZ
response_options.description: Cooperate with UNPROFOR collection-point inventories. Withdraw any ARBiH heavy weapons inside the 20km exclusion zone. Publicly support NATO enforcement against the VRS. Accept the symmetric application of the HWEZ regime as the diplomatic cost of credible Western coercion. This is the documented Sarajevo posture — the Presidency frames the ultimatum as long-overdue Western action and absorbs the relatively low material cost of symmetric application.

future_consequences.label: HWEZ cooperation posture follow-through
future_consequences.explanation: Sarajevo's documented HWEZ cooperation strengthens the diplomatic conditions for the March 1994 Washington Agreement framework and aligns Sarajevo's posture with the NATO-enforcement track that runs through R13 Deliberate Force compliance in 1995. The 12 February 1994 first-day-without-casualty since April 1992 is publicly owned by the Presidency as vindication of the NATO-enforcement posture (UN A/54/549 §§ on Sarajevo HWEZ regime; BB Vol. II Sarajevo siege chronology).

response_options.label: Refuse symmetric application — protest HWEZ to ARBiH
response_options.description: Publicly object to the symmetric framing's moral-equivalence of victim and aggressor. Refuse ARBiH heavy-weapon withdrawal from the exclusion zone while still benefiting from NATO action against the VRS. Counterfactual posture-of-protest: Assembly-debate currents (1994) on the moral-equivalence framing become the Presidency's recorded position. This jeopardizes Western support and the federation/Washington track that arrives in March; ICFY Co-Chairmen and Washington read the protest as obstructing the only effective coercion against RS.

future_consequences.label: HWEZ refusal posture follow-through
future_consequences.explanation: Sarajevo's HWEZ refusal carries international-standing and negotiating-leverage costs that propagate into the March 1994 Washington Agreement deliberations and the federation-track readiness conditions. Per Phase A B9 worksheet §5, the federation framework was historically achieved despite RBiH-Western friction, so the closure of federation precursors is soft rather than direct; the diplomatic conditions on the Washington decision shift adversely without statically blocking the row.

RS.headline: Sarajevo accepts NATO HWEZ symmetric application
RS.body: RBiH cooperates with UNPROFOR collection-point inventories and publicly supports NATO enforcement. Pale faces a consolidated diplomatic posture in Sarajevo and the credible threat of air strikes if the VRS does not comply with the 21 February deadline.

HRHB.headline: RBiH supports NATO Sarajevo ultimatum
HRHB.body: Sarajevo's Presidency accepts the symmetric HWEZ regime and cooperates with UNPROFOR. Mostar reads the move as a Federation-aligned diplomatic posture that strengthens the Washington track.

RS.headline: Sarajevo protests symmetric HWEZ application
RS.body: RBiH refuses ARBiH heavy-weapon withdrawal under the moral-equivalence framing. Pale reads the protest as friction in the Western coalition and weakening of Sarajevo's negotiating leverage.

HRHB.headline: RBiH refuses symmetric NATO ultimatum
HRHB.body: Sarajevo's Presidency objects to the HWEZ regime's symmetric application. Mostar weighs whether the protest strengthens or weakens the Federation track now under final US shuttle pressure.

title: Sarajevo Exclusion Zone Takes Effect
narrative: Under threat of NATO air strikes, the VRS begins withdrawing heavy weapons from a 20-kilometer exclusion zone around Sarajevo. Hundreds of artillery pieces and mortars are moved or placed under UNPROFOR control at collection points. On February 12, Sarajevo experiences its first day without a single casualty since April 1992. The siege is not lifted, but its deadliest instrument is temporarily muzzled.

effects.text: VRS heavy weapons are withdrawn from around Sarajevo. The exclusion zone brings the first sustained relief to the besieged capital.

historical_source: ICTY Karadzic Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), paras. 3521-3524. UNSCR 836. BB Vol. II.

title: NATO Shoots Down Serb Aircraft
narrative: NATO F-16 fighters intercept six VRS aircraft violating the no-fly zone over central Bosnia, shooting down four. The incident — NATO's first combat action in its forty-five-year history — signals a shift from passive observation to active enforcement. The VRS command begins to factor NATO air power into its operational calculations.

effects.text: NATO shoots down four of six VRS aircraft violating the no-fly zone. The alliance demonstrates its willingness to use force for the first time.

title: Washington Agreement — Pale's Non-Engagement
narrative: Washington shuttle diplomacy (Christopher, Galbraith, Redman) has produced a bipolar Federation framework between Sarajevo and Mostar — the Croat-Muslim peace and constitutional architecture of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Belgrade has been informed; Pale has not been invited. Karadzic and Krajisnik read the framework as a constraint on the Six Strategic Goals: a Federation entity occupying 51 percent of Bosnia narrows the corridor, contests the Drina-valley axis, and forecloses Sarajevo division ahead of any negotiated map. The Pale Assembly must record its written posture toward the Washington track: reject the bipolar Federation as the documented historical line, propose a trilateral alternative that brings RS into a parallel republic frame, condition any engagement on territorial recognition of the Six Goals platform, or accept observer status to maintain a channel to the framework Belgrade has not yet endorsed against.

effect.text: The Pale Assembly records its posture toward the Washington Agreement — the bipolar Federation framework concluded without RS participation.

source_note: RS was not a party to the Washington Agreement (1 + 18 March 1994). Karadzic and the Pale leadership read the bipolar Federation framework as a constraint on the Six Strategic Goals platform and treated the diplomatic track as instrumentally hostile rather than worth engaging; the documented historical posture is non-engagement (reject_federation) rather than a counter-proposal or observer-status overture. The X5 packet completes the Washington Agreement cross-faction trio: B10 (`rbih_washington_agreement_1994`, Packet 8) RBiH side; H9 (`hrhb_washington_agreement_1994`, Packet 7) HRHB side; this row RS side. All three are gated on Washington's calendar window (turn 99-102) and on the responding faction's foundational flag (X1 London Conference / X2 Vance-Owen / X3 Owen-Stoltenberg / X4 Contact Group cross-faction pattern from Packets 6/25/28/29). §3.6 forward-looking guard: any future `csq_rs_washington_*` row consuming this row's outcomes MUST NOT re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, paramilitary deployment, hostage-taking, or any sensitive-act response option. The Washington Agreement aftermath did include ARBiH-HVO joint pressure on RS (the Federation military integration track culminating in Operation Storm and Operation Mistral in 1995); consequence rows must stay within constitutional/political-strategic scope, not propagandize ethnic-targeting or re-author atrocity surfaces — those remain canon-gated through their existing event surfaces (un_hostage_crisis_1995; deliberate_force_rs_compliance_1995; rs_drina_campaign family slugs; srebrenica_falls_1995). The Washington Agreement signing led historically to the Federation framework that bounded the 1995 joint operations against RS, not to direct RS-targeting cleansing. Engine vocabulary substitutions per memory/engine_dimension_vocabulary.md: Belgrade patron-confidence shifts captured via `patron_confidence`; international standing via `international_standing`; negotiating leverage via `negotiating_leverage`; alliance change with RBiH via `alliance_change` (Federation alliance proxy, scaled 0-1); cohesion damage via `internal_cohesion`.
staff_assessment: Rejection mirrors the documented Pale Assembly posture and preserves the Six Goals platform claims, but cedes the diplomatic frame entirely to the Federation. Trilateral proposal opens a structurally honest alternative but offends Belgrade by going around Milosevic; conditional engagement preserves the Six Goals platform while keeping a channel open at the cost of patron friction; observer status maximizes international standing at the steepest cohesion cost — Pale hawks read it as capitulation to a framework Karadzic has publicly disdained.
trigger_evidence: The Washington Agreement framework (1 + 18 March 1994) has reached the formal signing milestone.
RS was not invited to the framework; the Pale Assembly must record its written posture toward the bipolar Federation it sees as a constraint on the Six Goals platform.
Belgrade has been informed but has not endorsed Pale's response; the patron channel is open for either alignment or defiance on this decision.

response_options.label: Reject the bipolar Federation
response_options.description: Karadzic and Krajisnik record the documented Pale position: the Washington Agreement is a constraint on the Six Strategic Goals platform. RS will not engage the bipolar framework, will not seek observer status, and will not propose a counter-frame; the Federation track is treated as hostile diplomatic territory. Belgrade is informed; the patron channel registers the rejection without alignment.

response_options.label: Propose a trilateral framework
response_options.description: Issue a Pale-side counter-proposal: replace the bipolar Federation with a tripartite framework that recognizes Republika Srpska as a constitutive entity alongside the Bosniak-Croat Federation. Belgrade is bypassed for the diplomatic initiative; Milosevic registers the move as Pale freelancing under Karadzic. International standing rises with the constructive posture; negotiating leverage opens; Federation alliance with RBiH frays slightly as the bipolar architecture is contested.

response_options.label: Engage conditionally
response_options.description: Indicate Pale will discuss the Washington framework if and only if it acknowledges the Six Strategic Goals — the corridor, the Drina-valley axis, Sarajevo division. Send Krajisnik to Geneva with a written brief; Belgrade is informed and consulted but the channel is Pale-led. The diplomatic posture is open without commitment; international standing rises modestly; Belgrade reads the move as freelance and registers mild patron friction.

response_options.label: Accept observer status
response_options.description: Acknowledge the bipolar Federation framework as a fact on the ground; accept observer status at the institutional working groups without contesting the constitutional architecture. The Six Strategic Goals platform breaks internally on this option — Pale hawks read observer status as capitulation to a framework Karadzic has publicly disdained. International standing rises sharply; internal cohesion takes the steepest hit. Belgrade tolerates but does not endorse the posture.

RBiH.headline: Pale ignores the Washington framework
RBiH.body: Karadzic and Krajisnik decline to engage the Federation track. Sarajevo reads the non-engagement as confirmation that RS will treat the Washington framework as hostile diplomatic territory; the Federation track strengthens by default.

HRHB.headline: RS refuses Washington engagement
HRHB.body: The Pale Assembly records non-engagement with the Federation framework. Mostar reads the move as the Six Goals platform staying intact; RS posture toward the joint anti-VRS Federation hardens.

RBiH.headline: Pale floats a tripartite counter-frame
RBiH.body: Karadzic proposes replacing the bipolar Federation with a tripartite framework that recognizes Republika Srpska alongside the Bosniak-Croat entity. Sarajevo reads the move as a serious diplomatic intervention that contests Washington's architecture; Belgrade is reported to be uneasy with Pale freelancing.

HRHB.headline: RS proposes trilateral framework
HRHB.body: Pale offers a counter-frame that recognizes Republika Srpska as a constitutive entity alongside the Federation. Mostar reads the proposal as a structural challenge to the Washington bipolar architecture; the Federation track gains friction.

RBiH.headline: Pale opens conditional channel
RBiH.body: RS indicates it will discuss the Washington framework if the Six Strategic Goals are acknowledged. Sarajevo reads the move as a posture-with-reservations that does not endorse the Federation but keeps a diplomatic channel open.

HRHB.headline: RS opens conditional engagement
HRHB.body: Krajisnik is dispatched to Geneva with a conditional brief tied to the Six Goals platform. Mostar reads the move as Pale temporizing without committing to the Federation framework.

RBiH.headline: Pale accepts Federation observer status
RBiH.body: RS acknowledges the bipolar Federation as a fact on the ground and takes observer status at the institutional working groups. Sarajevo reads the move as a structural concession; Pale hawks are reported to be in open dissent against Karadzic.

HRHB.headline: RS records observer-status acceptance
HRHB.body: Pale acknowledges the Federation framework without endorsing its constitutional architecture. Mostar reads the move as a partial capitulation that leaves the Six Goals platform internally fractured.

title: Washington Agreement Signed
narrative: Under heavy American pressure, Bosniak and Bosnian Croat leaders sign the Washington Agreement, ending the Croat-Bosniak war and establishing the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The agreement changes the military balance by creating a Federation framework against the VRS, though trust, command integration, and supply coordination remain uneven.
historical_source: Washington Agreement text, 1 + 18 March 1994; Vienna Framework Agreement, 26 March 1994; ICTY Prlic Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T) Vol. 1 §§452-470 (HR HB institutional continuity) and Vol. 3 §§120-200 (Tudjman transcripts and HR HB Presidency deliberations preceding the signing); Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II pp.451-455.
source_note: Balkan Battlegrounds frames Washington as an externally imposed but necessary Croat-Muslim peace and uneasy anti-VRS alliance, not immediate reconciliation. The OR-trigger on hrhb_political_goal ensures all three H1 branches reach the Washington Agreement decision: U.S. sanctions pressure transmitted via Tudjman makes acceptance the historical-default path regardless of which 1992 line the HZ HB Presidency selected (Prlic Vol. 3 §§120-200).
staff_assessment: Accepting the Federation framework ends the two-front Croat-Bosniak war and restores strategic room against the VRS, but staff should expect slow trust-building and uneven joint command.
trigger_evidence: The Croat-Bosniak war has begun in the event chain.
The formal Washington Agreement calendar milestone has arrived.

effects.text: The Washington Agreement ends the Croat-Bosniak war. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is established. HVO units rebuild cohesion under Federation military integration; HRHB-RBiH supply pipelines open.

response_options.description: Commit to the Federation framework, opening coordination and supply channels while former enemies integrate cautiously.

response_options.label: Accept with Reservations
response_options.description: Accept the agreement but maintain wariness toward former enemies. Slower integration but preserved autonomy.

RS.headline: Sarajevo embraces the Federation
RS.body: RBiH leadership commits fully to the formal Washington Agreement. Pale sees a consolidated Federation front, stronger international standing for Sarajevo, and reopened Croatian supply channels against the VRS.

HRHB.headline: Sarajevo commits to the Federation
HRHB.body: RBiH accepts the formal Washington framework without reservation. Mostar reads the move as a clear Federation commitment, with joint anti-VRS coordination and Croatian supply access now politically easier to sustain.

RS.headline: Sarajevo accepts with reservations
RS.body: RBiH signs onto the formal Washington Agreement while keeping distance from its former Croat adversaries. Pale still faces a Federation framework, but integration looks slower and more politically brittle.

HRHB.headline: RBiH enters Federation warily
HRHB.body: Sarajevo accepts the formal Washington settlement but signals continued caution toward former enemies. Mostar gains the Federation framework, though trust and operational integration will need time.

title: Washington Agreement — Sarajevo's Acceptance
narrative: Under cumulative US shuttle diplomacy (Christopher, Galbraith, Redman) and the post-Markale NATO ultimatum, the Sarajevo Presidency receives the Washington framework. Izetbegovic and Prime Minister Silajdzic delegate to Washington; the 1 March 1994 framework agreement and the 18 March 1994 constitutional agreement establish the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a parallel Preliminary Agreement on Confederation with Croatia witnessed by Tudjman. Acceptance ends the two-front Croat-Bosniak war and reopens Croatian supply lines, but Assembly hardliners and the Silajdzic-track skepticism record the acceptance as instrumental rather than ideological.
historical_source: Washington Framework Agreement, 1 March 1994 (signed in Washington D.C. by RBiH Prime Minister Haris Silajdzic, HRHB representative Kresimir Zubak, and Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic); Constitutional Agreement of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 18 March 1994 (signed at the White House by RBiH President Alija Izetbegovic, HRHB representative Kresimir Zubak, and Croatian President Franjo Tudjman); Preliminary Agreement on Confederation between the Republic of Croatia and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 18 March 1994; Vienna Framework Agreement, 26 March 1994; UN S/1994/308; ICTY Prosecutor v. Prlic et al. (IT-04-74-T) Trial Judgement Vol. 1 §§452-470 (Federation acceptance track and Bosnian Presidency deliberations) and Vol. 3 §§120-200 (Tudjman-Izetbegovic shuttle records); ICTY Prosecutor v. Karadzic (IT-95-5/18-T) Trial Judgement Vol. 1 (Bosnian Serb side reaction context); Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II pp. 451-455 (Sarajevo's instrumental acceptance posture); Bosnian Presidency Athens-channel records.
source_note: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II p. 451 frames Sarajevo's acceptance precisely as instrumental: a treaty 'essentially imposed from outside' that the Presidency 'had to seem to be agreeable' to in order to maintain international support and, more decisively, that 'allowed the ARBiH to end its desperate two-front war and concentrate on the crucial conflict with its Bosnian Serb foes.' Acceptance was real and operationally consequential — UNPROFOR took on cease-fire monitoring across Mostar, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Konjic, and Jablanica within days — but the political stake was instrumental rather than ideological. The OR-trigger on rbih_state_identity ensures all three B1 branches (civic, bosniak_national, pragmatic) reach the Washington decision: US shuttle pressure plus post-Markale NATO ultimatum makes acceptance the historical-default path regardless of which 1992 identity declaration the Sarajevo Presidency selected. This row is the RBiH-side companion to hrhb_washington_agreement_1994 (HRHB-side), per X5 composite worksheet ruling (Game Designer Wave 1: two separate per-faction events coordinated via runtime causality).
staff_assessment: Accepting the Federation framework ends the two-front Croat-Bosniak war, reopens Croatian supply lines, and restores diplomatic standing under US auspices, but staff should expect Assembly hardline objections and uneven joint command in the months that follow.
trigger_evidence: The Croat-Bosniak war has reached its diplomatic terminus under US shuttle pressure.

effect.text: The Sarajevo Presidency receives the Washington framework and must decide its posture toward the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

effects.text: Sarajevo's Presidency convenes to deliberate the Washington Agreement framework. Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, and the Assembly inner circle weigh acceptance against the cost of perpetuating the two-front war.

response_options.description: Commit fully to the Washington Agreement — sign the 1 March framework, the 18 March constitutional agreement, and accept the Confederation framework with Croatia. End the Croat-Bosniak war and reopen Croatian supply lines for the campaign against the VRS.

future_consequences.label: Federation framework acceptance follow-through
future_consequences.explanation: Sarajevo's signature on the Washington framework opens the federation military integration track and positions ARBiH for the 1995 joint offensives (Storm, Mistral, Sana) alongside HVO and HV forces. Croatian supply lines reopen; UNPROFOR cease-fire monitoring takes effect across Mostar, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Konjic, and Jablanica within days (BB Vol. II p. 451).

response_options.label: Accept under reservations
response_options.description: Sign the framework under US shuttle pressure but with the Silajdzic-track skepticism on record. The framework holds; execution friction will be higher; Assembly hardliners get the political cover they sought.

future_consequences.label: Federation framework with reservations
future_consequences.explanation: Same direction as accept (per BB Vol. II p. 451 — both options are forms of acceptance), but at a different posture. Silajdzic-track skepticism dampens commitment; the federation military integration track still opens but with friction. Counterfactual gradient capturing the same-direction-different-posture register documented in BB Vol. II p. 451.

title: Gorazde Crisis
narrative: The VRS launches a major offensive against the Gorazde safe area, overrunning UN observation posts and pushing into the outskirts of the town. Limited NATO air strikes prove insufficient to halt the advance. The crisis exposes the hollow nature of safe area protection and the mismatch between UN mandates and military reality.

effects.text: The VRS attacks the Gorazde safe area. Limited NATO strikes fail to stop the offensive, exposing the fragility of safe area protection.

title: Washington to Sarajevo: Don't Exploit the Military Window
narrative: Western capitals warn Izetbegović not to launch aggressive offensives in the wake of the Washington Agreement. Dramatic ARBiH advances would destabilize the federation, hand RS propaganda victories, and jeopardize the Contact Group process.
historical_source: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I pp.21-22; Washington Agreement text, Mar. 18 1994; Contact Group diplomacy chronology, May-July 1994.
source_note: Balkan Battlegrounds traces the post-Washington diplomatic lane through Federation institution-building, Contact Group shuttle diplomacy, ceasefire pressure, and the 51/49 settlement framework.
staff_assessment: Acknowledging the Western warning preserves patron confidence after Washington, but it costs Sarajevo some negotiating leverage and frustrates commanders who see a military opening.
trigger_evidence: The turn 106-114 window follows the formal Washington Agreement period.
The same diplomatic lane leads into Contact Group pressure and ceasefire proposals rather than unrestricted Federation offensives.

effect.text: Western capitals warn Sarajevo not to exploit the post-Washington military window with aggressive offensives.

response_options.label: Acknowledge the message
response_options.description: Historical posture: temper offensive planning to keep Western support intact. Patron confidence +8, negotiating leverage -5, internal cohesion -3.

response_options.label: Maintain our position
response_options.description: Keep pressure on the front despite Western caution. Patron confidence -10, negotiating leverage +6, military credibility +3.

This row's consequence lane stays within legitimate command-structure / patron-axis posture. Engine vocabulary substitutions per memory/engine_dimension_vocabulary.md: full_integration → alliance_change +0.20 (Federation alliance proxy) + internal_cohesion -10 (Croat nationalist faction friction) + patron_confidence -5 (Zagreb loses HVO command lever) + military_credibility +5; selective_integration → alliance_change +0.05 + internal_cohesion -5 + negotiating_leverage -5; parallel_commands (historical_default) → small alliance_change +0.05 + internal_cohesion -2 documenting the friction-tolerated status quo + military_credibility +2; refuse_integration → alliance_change -0.20 + patron_pressure +25 (US/Contact-Group anger) + patron_confidence +10 (Zagreb pleased) + international_standing -15 + recruitment_modifier 0.90× / 6 turns. This row is the HRHB-side companion to Packet 26's B11 (rbih_federation_army_integration_1994) per X5 composite worksheet ruling: two separate per-faction events coordinated via runtime causality.
staff_assessment: Parallel commands preserves HVO operational independence and the Zagreb patron channel but accepts the institutional friction cost; full integration captures US/Contact-Group patron reward and Federation alliance consolidation at the price of Croat nationalist faction friction and a Zagreb command-lever forfeit; selective integration splits the difference with thinner gains both ways; refuse integration ruptures the Washington framework and incurs a US patron-pressure spike plus international-standing collapse, with Zagreb pleased but Federation alliance shattered.
trigger_evidence: The Washington Agreement formally established the Federation Army (HVOBiH / VFBiH) on 1 + 18 March 1994.

ICRC and UNPROFOR field reports across Mostar, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Konjic, and Jablanica record persistent dual ARBiH-HVO command structures six months after the Federation Army's paper establishment.

US embassy archived reporting (Christopher / Galbraith / Redman channels) documents repeated Federation Army integration démarches awaiting a written Mostar posture; Tudjman-Susak correspondence admitted at Prlic Vol. 3 records Zagreb's preference for HVO retaining a parallel Croat command line.

response_options.label: Accept parallel commands (status quo)
response_options.description: Allow the Federation Army to remain a paper architecture: HVO and ARBiH brigades share the Federation table-of-organization slot but HVO retains its Mostar Defence Department chain, separate logistics depots, separate communications nets, and the Zagreb-Susak patron channel. Federation rhetoric outward, HVO operational independence inward — the documented historical posture through Vienna, the Contact Group framework, and Dayton.

response_options.label: Merge HVO and ARBiH into a unified Federation Army
response_options.description: Push full integration: shared chain of command, unified logistics, joint operational planning. HVO brigades subordinate to the Federation general staff. The Federation Army becomes the substantive military institution that Washington put on paper. US embassy and Contact Group reward the move with patron confidence; the Croat-nationalist current around Boban-successor leadership resents the dilution of HVO operational independence; Zagreb loses its parallel-command lever and Susak protests through the Tudjman channel.

response_options.label: Selective integration — shared staff, separate troops
response_options.description: Integrate at the Federation general-staff level (joint operational planning, shared intelligence) while keeping HVO and ARBiH troop formations under separate national chains. Mid-ground posture: thinner Federation alliance gain, thinner internal-cohesion cost, with negotiating-leverage forgone because the institutional ambiguity weakens Mostar's Dayton-track Federation argument.

response_options.label: Refuse Federation Army integration
response_options.description: Reject the Federation Army architecture entirely. HVO retains full institutional independence under the Mostar Defence Department and the Zagreb-Susak patron channel; ARBiH is treated as a parallel allied force, not a Federation Army peer. The Washington framework cracks at the Croat military-institution layer; US patron pressure surges; the Federation alliance proxy weakens. Zagreb is pleased — its parallel-command lever survives — but international standing collapses and the Contact Group framework loses its institutional anchor.

RS.headline: Mostar accepts parallel Federation commands
RS.body: HRHB allows the Federation Army architecture to remain on paper while HVO and ARBiH retain separate national chains. Pale assesses a Federation framework with persistent institutional friction on the Croat side; HVO military integration is nominal rather than substantive.

RBiH.headline: HVO retains parallel command chain
RBiH.body: Mostar accepts the parallel-commands status quo. Sarajevo reads the move as HVO preserving the Zagreb-Susak channel and the Mostar Defence Department line; the Federation Army architecture holds nominally without forcing institutional merger on the Croat side.

RS.headline: HVO merges under unified Federation command
RS.body: HRHB commits to full Federation Army integration on the Croat side. Pale faces a substantively unified Federation military structure with shared logistics and joint operational planning; the Washington framework gains institutional teeth and the HVO parallel chain dissolves.

RBiH.headline: Mostar accepts HVO-ARBiH merger
RBiH.body: HRHB commits to full Federation Army integration. Sarajevo welcomes the substantive merger; HVO subordinates to the Federation general staff and the Zagreb-Susak channel loses its parallel-command lever.

RS.headline: Mostar proposes selective Federation integration
RS.body: HRHB integrates Federation Army staff functions on the Croat side while keeping HVO troop formations under the Mostar Defence Department chain. Pale reads the move as mid-ground Federation consolidation with institutional ambiguity preserved on the Croat side.

RBiH.headline: Federation Army splits the difference on Croat side
RBiH.body: Mostar proposes shared staff with separate troops. Sarajevo sees a Federation framework that integrates intelligence and planning while preserving HVO national-chain operational control.

RS.headline: Mostar refuses Federation Army merger
RS.body: HRHB rejects the Federation Army architecture entirely on the Croat side. Pale assesses Washington framework friction at the institutional core; US patron pressure on Mostar surges, but the Federation alliance proxy weakens and Zagreb's parallel-command lever survives.

RBiH.headline: HVO breaks with Federation Army
RBiH.body: HRHB refuses Federation Army integration. Sarajevo sees the Washington framework cracking at the military-institution layer; HVO is treated as a parallel allied force under the Zagreb-Susak channel, not a Federation Army peer.

title: Belgrade Breaks with Pale
narrative: Milosevic has had enough. After the Bosnian Serb assembly rejects the Contact Group plan, Belgrade imposes sanctions on Republika Srpska, closing the border to military supplies and severing the political lifeline that has sustained the war effort. Your army's supply lines from Serbia are now severed. The international community watches to see if this is real or theater.
source_note: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II summarizes the Belgrade-Pale break after the Contact Group crisis.
staff_assessment: Pale leadership can hold its rejectionist line by defying Belgrade, but the choice trades internal cohesion for sharper supply pressure and a weaker patron relationship.
trigger_evidence: The Contact Group plan has entered the event chain.
Belgrade sanctions follow the RS rejection of the map.

effects.text: Belgrade imposes an embargo on Republika Srpska. The border with Serbia is closed to military supplies.

response_options.label: Seek accommodation with Belgrade
response_options.description: Open back-channels to Milosevic. Signal willingness to reconsider the Contact Group map. The embargo may be softened.

response_options.label: Defy Belgrade
response_options.description: We do not need Belgrade's permission to defend our people. Reject the Contact Group map and accept the consequences.

future_consequences.label: Belgrade split hardens
future_consequences.explanation: Defying Belgrade records rs_belgrade_response as defiant. No current catalog follow-up event directly keys on this value, but the branch remains visible in decision diagnostics.

RBiH.headline: Pale defies Belgrade embargo
RBiH.body: RS rejects Belgrade's pressure and accepts deeper isolation over the Contact Group map. Sarajevo sees a harder Pale line, but also a widening split between RS leadership and its Serbian patron.

HRHB.headline: RS stands against Belgrade
HRHB.body: Pale chooses defiance despite the border closure and military-supply shock. Mostar sees RS cohesion harden internally while patron confidence and international standing deteriorate.

RBiH.headline: Pale seeks accommodation with Belgrade
RBiH.body: RS opens back-channel accommodation with Milosevic and signals room to revisit the Contact Group map. Sarajevo sees possible relief for RS supply pressure, but also internal strains inside Pale.

HRHB.body: Pale looks for a way back toward Belgrade after the embargo. Mostar sees reduced immediate supply shock for RS if talks hold, at the cost of visible internal cohesion.

title: Anti-Sniping Agreement in Sarajevo
narrative: An anti-sniping agreement is reached for Sarajevo, aiming to reduce the daily toll of civilians killed by snipers along the city's exposed boulevards and intersections. Compliance is sporadic, but the agreement represents a small step in civilian protection and provides UNPROFOR with additional monitoring authority.
source_note: Existing event/essay/project sources ground the row's institutional and diplomatic context. This note adds no casualty figures, causal claims, prohibited player choices, or alternate-outcome prevention framing.

effect.text: An anti-sniping agreement is signed for Sarajevo. Compliance is uneven but civilian casualties decrease temporarily.

title: 5th Corps Breaks Out of Bihac
narrative: Sarajevo Presidency files, autumn 1994. General Atif Dudakovic and the 5th Corps in Bihac are the principal armed expression of the Sarajevo line against the Fikret Abdic / APWB split declared at Velika Kladusa on 27 September 1993. Dudakovic has presented an offensive plan: push from the pocket into Grabez and toward Bosanska Krupa against the VRS, while overrunning APWB-held Velika Kladusa to the north. The political record is in your hands. Press the offensive, hold the perimeter, seek negotiation with APWB and indirect channels to RS/RSK, or accept ceasefire terms that would functionally recognize the APWB split.

effect.text: The Sarajevo Presidency records a 5th Corps Bihac-pocket posture for autumn 1994.

effects.text: Dudakovic and the 5th Corps await the Sarajevo political record on the autumn-1994 Bihac-pocket posture.

source_note: B6 worksheet 2026-05-27 + v1.3 packet §3.6 forward-looking guard: B6 is Ring-2 operational/posture (no atrocity authorization surface). Any future `csq_rbih_bihac_*` row consuming `bihac_5th_corps_1994_response` outcomes MUST NOT re-author atrocity authorization, cleansing, hostage-taking, or any sensitive-act response option. Cost floors on `consolidate_defend` and `accept_ceasefire_terms` per Game Designer Wave 1 review on packet v1.1 edit 13 prevent counterfactual dominance of the historical `press_offensive` line. BB Vol. II pp. 406-417 region (Bihac 1994 chronology, 5th Corps offensive, October high-water mark, November-December counter-attack), UNSCR 958 of 19 November 1994 (NATO close-air-support authority extended to Bihac safe area), NATO 21 November 1994 Udbina airfield close-air-support action.
staff_assessment: Pressing the offensive mirrors the documented Dudakovic posture and the historical APWB liquidation (briefly) at Velika Kladusa in late October 1994; the strategic value lies in eliminating the APWB rear threat and catalyzing the international engagement decision tree leading to Operation Storm 1995 and Mistral/Sana 1995. Consolidating the defense reduces immediate casualties but permits APWB persistence and weakens 5th Corps political-recruit posture into 1995. Seeking negotiation signals conditional military pressure to APWB and RS. Accepting ceasefire terms functionally recognizes the APWB split, sharply degrades 5th Corps capability for 1995 operations, and pays a federation-level cohesion cost.
trigger_evidence: The 5th Corps offensive plan from Dudakovic is before the Presidency.
APWB at Velika Kladusa and VRS positions on Grabez/Bosanska Krupa axis define the autumn-1994 operational picture.
The Bihac pocket is supplied only through the RSK-controlled UNPROFOR corridor and HVO; political-military posture for autumn 1994 is in question.

response_options.label: Press the offensive — push Grabez, overrun Velika Kladusa
response_options.description: Authorize Dudakovic's plan. 5th Corps presses into Grabez and toward Bosanska Krupa against VRS positions while overrunning APWB-held Velika Kladusa. The advance achieves operational momentum into late October; the joint VRS/RSK/APWB counter-attack from November rolls the gains back, and the pocket survives only via NATO close-air-support escalation on 21 November 1994.

effects.text: The 5th Corps advances from the Bihac pocket toward the Grabez and Grmec approaches before the later joint counteroffensive.

response_options.label: Consolidate the defense — hold the perimeter
response_options.description: Refuse Dudakovic's offensive plan. The 5th Corps holds the Bihac perimeter and does not press into Grabez or against APWB. Immediate casualties drop; APWB persists at Velika Kladusa through 1994-1995; the 5th Corps' political-recruit posture softens without the offensive-momentum narrative. The autumn-1994 NATO escalation decision tree does not engage on the Bihac axis.

response_options.label: Seek negotiation — open Bihac-pocket ceasefire channels
response_options.description: Direct Dudakovic to open talks with APWB on a Bihac-pocket ceasefire, with indirect channels to RS/RSK. Sarajevo's military pressure on the pocket axis is signaled as conditional. Talks open; no resolution arrives; the autumn-1994 operational picture stalls without the offensive momentum and without the immediate political cost of full recognition.

response_options.label: Accept ceasefire terms — concede Velika Kladusa to APWB
response_options.description: Accept the counter-attackers' terms in advance: territorial concession to APWB at Velika Kladusa, halt of all 5th Corps offensive operations. The crisis is averted without NATO escalation. The cost is functional recognition of the APWB split, sharply degraded 5th Corps capability for 1995 operations, and federation-level cohesion damage. The 5th Corps cadres read the decision as Sarajevo betrayal at the moment of crisis.

RS.headline: Sarajevo authorizes 5th Corps Bihac offensive
RS.body: The Presidency clears Dudakovic to press Grabez and overrun Velika Kladusa. Pale reads the decision as Sarajevo committing to a Bihac-axis military solution; VRS coordinates the counter-attack with RSK and APWB.

HRHB.headline: 5th Corps cleared for autumn-1994 offensive
HRHB.body: Sarajevo authorizes the Bihac-pocket offensive. Mostar reads the decision as Sarajevo holding the line against the Abdic split and signals continued Federation military coordination.

RS.headline: Sarajevo refuses 5th Corps offensive
RS.body: The Presidency holds Dudakovic to a defensive posture. Pale reads the decision as Sarajevo tolerating the APWB existence; pressure on the eastern enclaves rises as the Bihac axis quiets.

HRHB.headline: RBiH adopts defensive Bihac posture
HRHB.body: Sarajevo holds the 5th Corps to the perimeter. Mostar notes the softer Sarajevo line on the internal Bosniak fracture and the absent NATO escalation on the Bihac axis.

RS.headline: Sarajevo seeks Bihac-pocket ceasefire channels
RS.body: The Presidency opens talks with APWB and indirect channels through RSK. Pale reads the signal as Sarajevo's military pressure on the Bihac axis being conditional.

HRHB.headline: RBiH opens Bihac ceasefire negotiations
HRHB.body: Sarajevo seeks talks with APWB and indirect RS/RSK channels. Mostar weighs the precedent for federation-level negotiation discipline.

RS.headline: Sarajevo accepts Bihac ceasefire terms
RS.body: The Presidency concedes Velika Kladusa to APWB and halts 5th Corps offensive operations. Pale reads the decision as the Sarajevo line breaking on the internal Bosniak fracture; the autumn-1994 NATO escalation does not arrive.

HRHB.headline: RBiH accepts APWB-favorable ceasefire
HRHB.body: Sarajevo accepts the counter-attackers' terms. Mostar notes the federation-level cohesion damage and the degraded 5th Corps capability for 1995 operations.

title: Operation Cincar — Kupres Falls to HVO
narrative: The HVO, reinforced by Croatian Army units, launches Operation Cincar against VRS positions around Kupres. After fierce fighting in mountainous terrain, Kupres falls on November 3. The operation captures a strategically vital junction that threatens VRS supply routes to Donji Vakuf. The Washington Agreement's military dividend is becoming apparent.

effects.text: Kupres falls to HVO forces in Operation Cincar. VRS supply routes in western Bosnia are threatened.

historical_source: BB Vol. II, Ch. 11. ICTY Prlic et al. (IT-04-74-T). Croatian operational records.

title: Bihac Crisis Deepens
narrative: The VRS, supported by forces from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Abdic's APWB militia, launches a major counteroffensive against the Bihac pocket. The 5th Corps is pushed back toward the town itself, and the crisis threatens the complete fall of the enclave. NATO air strikes against VRS airfields prove too limited to change the situation.

effects.text: The Bihac pocket faces collapse as VRS and allied forces close in. NATO strikes prove inadequate to lift the siege.

title: UN Arms Embargo Enforcement Ebbs
narrative: The UN General Assembly approves a nonbinding resolution calling for the Bosnian arms embargo to be lifted if the Bosnian Serbs reject the Contact Group plan. The embargo remains on paper, but Washington's enforcement posture has changed; Bosnian government supply channels begin to widen.

effect.text: The embargo is not formally gone, but enforcement against Bosnia is loosening.

title: Carter Brokers Winter Ceasefire
narrative: Jimmy Carter arrives in Sarajevo. The former president, acting as private mediator, shuttles between the warring parties and extracts a commitment to a complete cessation of hostilities effective New Year's Day. Humanitarian corridors will reopen. Behind the scenes, both sides know the ceasefire is a breathing space — time to rearm, resupply, and prepare for whatever comes next.
source_note: Carter Center archives, Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II Ch. 12, and the ICTY Karadzic Judgment ground the winter COHA.
staff_assessment: Sarajevo can preserve diplomatic credibility by honoring the Carter pause, while using the lower tempo to rebuild under scrutiny.
trigger_evidence: External diplomatic calendar: Carter's December 1994 Sarajevo-Pale shuttle and the COHA are modeled as a fixed late-December event.
The turn 138-139 window is an exogenous calendar guardrail, not a battlefield-state predicate.

effect.text: A four-month cessation of hostilities is agreed. The guns fall temporarily silent across Bosnia.

response_options.label: Honor the ceasefire
response_options.description: Use the pause to resupply and rebuild. Comply with the agreement's terms. International credibility improves.

response_options.label: Use the pause to prepare offensives
response_options.description: Nominally comply while aggressively repositioning forces and stockpiling supplies. The spring offensive will be stronger.

RS.headline: Sarajevo honors Carter ceasefire
RS.body: RBiH signals compliance with the winter cessation of hostilities and uses the pause to rebuild. Pale sees lower immediate offensive pressure and improved international standing for Sarajevo.

HRHB.headline: RBiH respects winter ceasefire
HRHB.body: Sarajevo commits to honoring the Carter pause while resupplying and rebuilding. Mostar sees the Federation side preserving diplomatic credibility during the temporary quiet.

RS.headline: Sarajevo prepares under ceasefire cover
RS.body: RBiH nominally accepts the winter pause while stockpiling and repositioning for future operations. Pale sees a stronger spring threat and some erosion in Sarajevo's international standing.

HRHB.headline: RBiH uses the pause for force buildup
HRHB.body: Sarajevo treats the ceasefire as a chance to prepare for later offensives. Mostar sees stronger Federation military prospects, with diplomatic risk if the posture becomes too visible.
